analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 50% excise tax on large oil companies' windfall crude oil profits and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the Senate and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax large oil companies — those extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels of crude oil per day — 50% of each barrel's price above a 2015-2019 baseline average of Brent crude, adjusted for inflation. All revenue collected would go into a trust fund and be paid back to individual taxpayers as a rebate, phasing down for higher incomes and phasing out above $75,000 for single filers and $150,000 for joint filers. The tax would apply retroactively to oil removed or imported after the end of 2021, capturing the windfall profits oil companies earned during the 2022 price spike.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers, especially lower- and middle-income households. The rebate is fully refundable, so even people with little or no income tax liability would receive it, and it phases down only for higher incomes — shrinking for individuals above $75,000 and for joint filers above $150,000.

how_it_helps.text: A 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil priced above its 2015-2019 average would capture a share of the extraordinary profits large oil companies earned when energy prices spiked, and the revenue would be returned to taxpayers rather than kept by producers [S2][S3].

The rebate is structured like the stimulus checks of 2021: it is refundable, joint filers receive 150% of the individual amount, and it phases down by 5% of income above $75,000 (single), $112,500 (head of household), or $150,000 (joint), so the money goes mainly to ordinary households [S3].

The tax reaches companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels daily — the largest producers and importers — and applies with aggregation rules so affiliated companies cannot escape the threshold by splitting themselves up [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers and importers, which would owe the 50% tax on each barrel sold above the baseline price. To the extent oil companies pass some of the tax through to prices at the pump, consumers would share the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big crude oil producers and importers

drawbacks.text: A windfall tax on oil producers can be passed through to consumers: to the extent companies raise prices to cover the tax, drivers at the pump pay part of it back, partially offsetting the rebate [S3].

Applying the tax retroactively to crude removed or imported after December 31, 2021 would tax activity that was already undertaken, which critics argue deters future investment in domestic oil production when supply is tight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct design favors ordinary households: the largest producers and importers owe the tax, and the proceeds are rebated with the biggest checks going to lower- and middle-income filers. The main real cost is that producers may pass some of the tax through to gasoline prices, and a retroactive levy on 2022 sales could discourage investment in new production — a trade-off supporters considered worth making but which the Senate never weighed, because the bill never got a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: Whitehouse introduced it on February 14, 2023, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on February 14, 2023 [S1][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of record [S5].
Eighteen senators — 17 Democrats and 1 Independent — cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no further committee action and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large crude oil producers and importers came out ahead: they never faced the tax, which was never even taken up by the Finance Committee. With no Senate Republican cosponsors and the bill stalled in committee controlled by the other party's calendar — the Finance Committee chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) — the bill sat untouched for two years until Congress adjourned.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large crude oil producers and importers

for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor

for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Brown, Warren, Sanders, Stabenow, Booker, Kaine, Murphy, and Casey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from 17 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 14, 2023 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years it had majority-party support, allowing it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Senate Republican supported the bill, and with the bill parked in committee the full chamber never voted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: Companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels daily would owe a 50% excise tax on each barrel priced above its 2015-2019 average, retroactive to sales after the end of 2021. Because the bill never advanced, these companies kept the full windfall profits from the 2022 price spike instead of sharing them with taxpayers.
